title: A more transactional international order and thinner public capacity are turning trust, foresight, and AI literacy into core state capabilities
source_unit: Salzburg Global, Our Key Insights: Public Institutions Responding to a New Era: Strategy in a Transformed Global Landscape, September 11, 2026
geography: International public-sector strategy discussion with regional perspectives from Europe, North America, and developing-country contexts

observations.period: September 2026; international order and public strategy

denominator.unit: Salzburg Global Public Sector Strategy Network synthesis

order_shift.value: the publication describes a movement from a postwar expectation that shared rules create mutual benefit toward more transactional state relationships aimed at extracting advantage

diversification.value: developing countries are described as diversifying away from Western-centric frameworks and forming new alliances

strategic_implication.value: public institutions are asked to treat strategic adaptation as a capability under constraint rather than as a one-off crisis response

observations.method: Salzburg Global facilitated retreat and editorial synthesis of senior public-sector leaders, strategic advisers, and policy experts.
observations.uncertainty: This is a curated expert synthesis, not a systematic measure of state behavior, alliance diversification, or the relative prevalence of transactional diplomacy.
observations.subgroup: Public institutions, strategic leaders, developing-country governments, Western governments, and communities affected by geopolitical and institutional change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Transactional bargaining can coexist with durable cooperation, and alliance diversification may reflect pragmatic risk management rather than rejection of Western institutions.

observations.period: September 2026; state capacity and dependence on private actors

capacity_loss.value: the publication argues that decades of disinvestment have eroded core in-house expertise in Western governments

private_dependence.value: reduced internal capacity is linked to greater dependence on private actors for strategic and operational capability

end_to_end_test.value: the relevant test is whether public institutions retain enough expertise to set direction, evaluate vendors, learn, and remain accountable after outsourcing

observations.method: Expert discussion and policy synthesis focused on public-sector strategy, institutional capability, and long-term change.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not quantify capacity loss, compare outsourcing outcomes, or establish that private provision necessarily reduces public value.
observations.subgroup: Civil services, public managers, vendors, contractors, elected leaders, and residents dependent on public systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Private partners can add specialized capability when governments preserve procurement expertise, transparency, public ownership of goals, and effective oversight.

observations.period: September 2026; AI, foresight, and institutional literacy

ai_literacy.value: AI investment is framed as requiring substantive literacy, not only technical deployment or procurement

foresight.value: strategic foresight is framed as a distributed societal capacity rather than a specialist function held by a central unit

education.value: education systems are urged to support human flourishing and judgment as technology and geopolitical conditions change

observations.method: Seven-point synthesis from a cross-regional public-sector strategy retreat.
observations.uncertainty: These are strategic recommendations and do not show which literacy or foresight interventions improve decisions, employment, trust, or distributional outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Public servants, educators, students, technology users, civic organizations, and communities exposed to AI-mediated decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Distributed foresight and broad AI literacy can become diffuse responsibilities without time, funding, decision rights, or measurable accountability.

observations.period: September 2026; institutional trust and durable change

denominator.unit: Salzburg Global public-trust and change framework

trust_route.value: trust in public institutions is framed as needing actionable inclusion and solid evidence rather than messaging alone

change_horizon.value: sustained change is linked to long-term commitments and leadership character rather than short-cycle announcements

open_test.value: follow inclusion from participation into changed decisions, implementation capacity, visible evidence, and durable public legitimacy

observations.method: Expert synthesis of public-sector strategy discussions on trust, leadership, evidence, and durable change.
observations.uncertainty: The publication does not evaluate specific participation mechanisms or establish causal effects on trust or implementation.
observations.subgroup: Public institutions, affected communities, civil society, elected leaders, public workers, and private partners.
observations.counterinterpretation: Participation and evidence can increase procedural burden or slow decisions unless institutions clarify tradeoffs, authority, and feedback loops.

related_sources.claim: Related Salzburg Global cultural-infrastructure work provides a complementary route from public meaning and cultural capacity to institutional trust.
OECD cross-national trust evidence provides a quantitative comparison for voice, service experience, complex decisions, and AI governance.

boundary: This record adds a comparative geopolitical-institutional route from a more transactional global order and thinner public capacity through state expertise, private dependence, AI literacy, distributed foresight, inclusion, and trust. It is a curated expert synthesis, not representative public opinion, a causal evaluation of state capacity, or proof that any proposed capability improves outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Salzburg Global September 11, 2026 publication page was reviewed for the transactional-order diagnosis, alliance diversification, public-capacity erosion, private dependence, seven key insights, AI literacy, distributed foresight, long-term change, and trust through inclusion and evidence.
